content: The Action for Nutrition initiative (2016–2020) and the six global nutrition targets for 2025, adopted by the World Health Assembly in 2012, represent significant milestones in addressing global nutrition challenges. Additionally, a series of voluntary targets for the prevention and control of noncommunicable diseases (NCDs) were established in alignment with the Political Declaration of the first high-level meeting of the General Assembly on NCD prevention and control. This culminated in the adoption of the Global Action Plan for the Prevention and Control of NCDs (2013–2020) by the World Health Assembly, which includes nine voluntary global targets, such as a 25% relative reduction in premature mortality from NCDs by 2025. Unhealthy diets are recognized as one of the four major behavioral risk factors for NCDs. Several countries have implemented integrated actions to support nutrition and reduce NCDs. These include taking responsibility for food value chains, introducing economic incentives, subsidies, and taxation measures to promote health, and increasing food biodiversity across production and supply chains. Enhancing dietary diversity through these measures is critical to reversing negative diet-related health outcomes, particularly among vulnerable and marginalized populations. For instance, linking local agricultural production with school feeding programs can generate income for smallholder households, conserve biodiversity, and improve access to quality, nutritious diets for underprivileged school-aged children. While progress has been made in increasing access to safe and nutritious foods in some areas, more coordinated, cross-sectoral action is required to address the growing burden of malnutrition and diet-related NCDs. The concept of mainstreaming biodiversity refers to integrating biodiversity conservation and sustainable use into all stages of policymaking, planning, programming, and implementation. The goal is to reduce the negative impacts of productive sectors, development investments, and human activities on biodiversity. This guidance does not aim to provide an exhaustive overview of scientific findings but builds upon them with relevant examples. It identifies six essential building blocks and entry points for mainstreaming biodiversity to achieve healthy, diverse, and sustainable diets. The publication is divided into three main parts. Part 1 explores the linkages between biodiversity, nutrition, and health, including the pressures and impacts of agrobiodiversity loss on food systems and their effects on nutrition and health outcomes. Part 2 outlines core building blocks to guide stakeholders in mainstreaming biodiversity into nutrition and health. It also highlights fundamental connections between food biodiversity, nutrition, and healthy diets, providing an indicative list of actions to support mainstreaming. These actions are intended as a starting point to be adapted and tailored to local and national contexts. Part 3 offers an indicative list of indicators for healthy and sustainable diets, which can be adapted and tested in different local contexts to assess baseline status and identify opportunities to strengthen biodiversity mainstreaming in nutrition. The report is complemented by a special report focusing on mainstreaming biodiversity for nutrition and health in Small Island Developing States (SIDS), contributing to the WHO Special Initiative on Climate and Health in SIDS. This additional report provides tailored background and examples specific to the unique vulnerabilities of small islands. Malnutrition in all its forms, including unhealthy diets, has been identified as the leading global health risk, surpassing the combined impacts of AIDS, malaria, and tuberculosis. As of 2018, an estimated 821 million people were undernourished, and the developmental, economic, social, and medical consequences of malnutrition are severe and long-lasting. Poor nutrition not only affects individual capacity but also hinders the development potential of entire communities. A new global nutritional reality has emerged, where undernutrition (wasting, stunting, and micronutrient deficiencies), overweight, obesity, and diet-related NCDs coexist within the same populations, households, and even individuals. This double burden of malnutrition has intergenerational implications, as maternal undernutrition and obesity are linked to poor health outcomes in offspring. The double burden is particularly significant in lowand middle-income countries, with overlapping forms of malnutrition affecting more than one-third of these nations, especially in sub-Saharan Africa, South Asia, East Asia, and the Pacific. While stunting has declined in recent years, other forms of malnutrition, such as childhood overweight and micronutrient deficiencies, remain unacceptably high or have increased. Globally, nearly one in three people suffer from one or more forms of malnutrition, and this is projected to rise to one in two by 2025 if current trends continue. Household-level double burden of malnutrition is primarily driven by the coexistence of overweight women and stunted children, with the prevalence of this combination increasing in many countries. By contrast, the prevalence of households with thin mothers and overweight children is extremely low, at less than 1% in most countries. The loss of biodiversity in global food systems poses a significant and growing threat to the availability and accessibility of healthy diets, particularly for vulnerable and marginalized populations. Human activities, including land-use changes, overexploitation, climate change, pollution, and invasive species, are the primary drivers of biodiversity loss. Deforestation and agricultural expansion are the leading direct drivers of biodiversity loss and significant contributors to climate change. These changes also drive the emergence of infectious diseases. The reduction of agrobiodiversity occurs as natural landscapes are converted for pasture, monoculture, or agricultural projects, often with negative impacts on ecosystem services. Agroecosystems play a critical role in sustaining food production, human nutrition, and ecosystem resilience. At the individual level, they contribute to microbial diversity in the gut microbiota, improve immunoregulation, and support inflammatory responses. At the landscape level, agroecosystems influence the delivery of essential ecosystem services, including crop productivity, the availability and safety of wild foods, and the regulation of water quality and availability. However, anthropogenic activities compound pressures on biodiversity and the ecosystem functions it sustains, with climate change acting as a threat multiplier. Biodiversity is a central link between nutrition and environmental sustainability. It provides the variety of essential foods, nutrients, vitamins, and minerals, as well as life-sustaining ecosystem services such as pollination and soil fertility. However, the biodiversity-related foundations of food production are in decline at every level. Two major mechanisms increasingly limit access to healthy and nutritious diets: the narrowing of available food varieties and breeds from managed agroecosystems (agrobiodiversity) and reduced access to sustainably harvested wild species. These pressures ultimately determine health outcomes at individual, household, and population levels, making equity central to addressing biodiversity loss and climate change and their impacts on nutrition and health.
